unit.title: Perform gas metal arc welding process to AWS specification (Pipe and plate)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

essays.stem: Explain the main differences between GMAW groove welding on plate and on pipe to the same AWS code. Cover the positions, the transfer mode, the fit-up, root control, testing and the welder's qualification.
essays.modelAnswer: On plate, the position stays the same along the joint, such as 1G, 3G or 4G. On fixed pipe, the position changes all the way round, from flat to vertical to overhead, so the welder must change the gun angle and speed as he goes. Plate joints are often welded on backing, such as ceramic tape or a steel strip, while pipe roots are usually open and need careful control of the gap, root face and keyhole. Plate in the flat can be welded with spray transfer, but pipe roots are usually short-circuit or pulsed, which can lack fusion if the technique is poor. Both are visually inspected and tested by bends or radiography, but pipe coupons are cut from set places round the pipe. A welder's qualification is limited by position, transfer mode and thickness; a pipe test may cover plate, but a plate test does not cover small pipe.
markingPoints: Position fixed on plate but changing round pipe
Backing on plate; open root on pipe with gap and keyhole control
Transfer mode differences and the lack-of-fusion risk
Testing differences, including strip locations on pipe
Qualification limits between pipe and plate

essays.stem: Describe how you would weld an open-root pipe joint in the 5G position with a downhill short-circuit GMAW root, to a WPS, and prepare it for the fill passes.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the WPS for the bevel, root face, gap, wire, gas, wire speed and voltage. I clean the bevels and the pipe inside and out, set an even gap and line the pipes up with no step, then tack and grind the tacks thin. I set the machine to the WPS and check the gas flow. I start at the top (12 o'clock) and weld down one side to just past the bottom, keeping a short, steady stick-out and the arc on the front of the pool so the wire fuses both edges and a small keyhole forms. I keep travel steady so the pool does not run ahead of the arc. Then I weld down the other side, overlapping the starts and stops. I clean the root and lightly grind the humps and edges so the next pass fuses well. I check the inside for full penetration before the hot pass.
markingPoints: Prepares, cleans, fits and tacks to the WPS
Starts at the top and welds each half downhill
Short, steady stick-out with the arc on the front of the pool
Joins starts and stops and keeps penetration even
Cleans and grinds the root and checks it before the next pass

essays.stem: Explain why short-circuit GMAW procedures and welders need special care under AWS codes, and how qualification tests show their welds are sound.
essays.modelAnswer: Short-circuit transfer puts in little heat, which is good for thin metal and roots, but the weld can lie on the side wall without fusing to it. This lack of fusion is often hidden inside and may not show on the surface or even on a radiograph. For this reason, many AWS structural codes do not let a short-circuit procedure be used as prequalified. It must be qualified by welding a test plate or pipe and testing it, and the results are recorded on a PQR. Welders are also qualified for the transfer mode they used, so a spray test does not cover short-circuit work. Bend tests are good at finding lack of fusion, because the strip opens up where the weld did not fuse. Macro etches show fusion at the side walls, and ultrasonic testing can find flat faults. Only when the tests pass is the WPS approved and the welder qualified.
markingPoints: Explains the lack of side-wall fusion risk
Not prequalified, so qualification by PQR
Welder qualification tied to the transfer mode
Bend tests and macros show lack of fusion
Ultrasonic testing for flat faults; approval only when tests pass

essays.stem: Describe how you would GMAW weld a single-V butt joint in 10 mm carbon steel plate in the 4G (overhead) position on ceramic backing, to a WPS.
essays.modelAnswer: I read the WPS for the groove angle, gap, wire, gas, transfer mode, wire speed and voltage. I bevel and clean the plates to bright metal, set the gap and fix the ceramic backing tape firmly under the joint so it is centred on the gap. I tack the plates and fix the coupon overhead at a comfortable height in the stand. I wear full PPE, with a cap and closed collar against falling spatter. I set the machine for short-circuit or pulsed transfer, as the WPS says, and check the gas flow. I weld the root with a short stick-out and a slight push, keeping the pool small so it does not sag, and letting it wet both edges and the backing. I clean between passes. Fill beads are laid as stringers or with small weaves, pausing at the toes. The cap is kept flat. I fill each crater, remove the backing after welding and check the root and cap.
markingPoints: Prepares, cleans, gaps and fixes the ceramic backing
Sets the transfer mode and settings from the WPS
Overhead PPE and stance
Keeps a small pool, fuses both edges, cleans between passes
Fills craters, removes the backing and inspects

essays.stem: Describe how you would GMAW weld a pipe-to-plate fillet in the 5F position and how the weld would be tested.
essays.modelAnswer: In 5F the pipe is fixed with its axis horizontal and the fillet runs round it, so the position changes from overhead to vertical to flat. I read the WPS, clean the pipe end and the plate, and set the pipe square to the plate, checking with a square. I tack in three or four places. I set the machine and gas to the WPS. I weld each half of the joint, starting near the bottom and going up to the top, or as the WPS directs. I aim the arc so both the pipe and the plate are fused, putting a little more heat on the thicker plate, and I change my gun angle as I go round. I keep the legs even and fill the craters. For testing, the weld is checked by eye and with a fillet gauge, then cut at several places round the pipe and etched, so the inspector can see fusion and leg size where the position changed.
markingPoints: Describes 5F and the changing position
Prepares, squares and tacks the pipe to the plate
Welds each half in the right direction to the WPS
Fuses both members and keeps even legs, filling craters
Tests by eye, gauge and macros cut round the pipe

essays.stem: Explain how you would record a PQR for a GMAW pipe procedure test: what you would measure, how you would measure it, and why each value matters.
essays.modelAnswer: I record the pipe grade, size and wall, and the joint design measured before welding: bevel angle, root face and gap. I record the wire class, size and batch, and the gas mix and flow rate from a flowmeter at the nozzle. For each pass I record the transfer mode, wire feed speed, voltage and current, measured with checked meters at the arc, not only the set's display, and the travel speed, found by timing a measured length of weld. I also note the position, direction (uphill or downhill), preheat and interpass temperature, using temperature crayons or a thermometer. These values matter because the WPS ranges are based on them, and a change in any key value may change the quality of the weld. After welding, I record the visual result and the results of the bend, macro or other tests. The record is signed by the welder and the witness.
markingPoints: Records pipe, joint design, wire and gas
Records transfer mode, wire speed, volts, amps for each pass
Uses checked meters and times travel speed
Records position, direction, preheat and interpass
Records test results and gets the record signed

essays.stem: Describe the hazards of GMAW welding of pipe and plate in a fabrication shop, and the controls you would put in place.
essays.modelAnswer: Heavy plate and pipe can fall or crush hands and feet, so we use lifting gear, safety boots and gloves, and chock pipe so it cannot roll. Turning rolls have nip points, so they are guarded and only the operator controls them. The GMAW arc gives off strong ultraviolet light and spatter, so welders wear a helmet with the right shade, flame-resistant clothes and gloves, and screens protect others. Fume is controlled with extraction at the arc and ventilation. Gas cylinders are chained upright and closed after use. The wire can shoot out when inched, so the gun is never pointed at anyone. Live parts and cables are checked before use and kept dry. Hot coupons are marked and handled with tongs. Spatter can start fires, so burnable things are cleared and an extinguisher is close. We follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Handling heavy plate and pipe, chocking
Rolls guarded and controlled
UV, spatter and fire controlled with PPE, screens and clearance
Fume extraction and cylinder care
Wire, electrical and hot-metal hazards controlled

essays.stem: Compare solid wire and metal-cored wire for GMAW of carbon steel pipe and plate. Say when you would choose each.
essays.modelAnswer: Solid wire is a plain steel wire, usually copper coated, with manganese and silicon to remove oxygen. It can be used in short-circuit, spray and pulsed transfer, works well for open roots on pipe and thin plate, and is cheaper. It leaves small glassy islands but no slag cover. Metal-cored wire is a thin steel tube filled mostly with metal powder. It carries current in its outer sheath, so it deposits metal faster than solid wire of the same size, with a wider, more forgiving arc and good side-wall fusion. It leaves very little slag, so cleaning between passes is quick. It costs more per kilogram. I would choose solid wire for pipe roots, thin plate and general work, and metal-cored wire for thicker plate fill and cap passes and long production runs where speed matters, as long as the WPS covers it.
markingPoints: Describes solid wire and its uses
Describes metal-cored wire construction
Higher deposit rate and good fusion with metal-cored
Cost and cleaning differences
Chooses each for a sensible job, within the WPS

essays.stem: As team leader, explain how you would plan and control the GMAW fabrication of 12 handrail posts (steel pipe welded to base plates) for a hotel in Negril, to a WPS and drawing.
essays.modelAnswer: I study the drawing for the pipe and plate sizes, fillet sizes and finish. I check that the WPS covers pipe-to-plate fillets in the positions we will use, and that each welder's WPQ covers them. I order the pipe, plate, wire and gas, and check them when they arrive. I make a jig so every post is set square to its base plate at the same height. I plan for most welding to be done with the post turned so the weld is in an easy position, such as 2F. To stop the base plates dishing, I clamp them down and weld in balanced parts. I inspect the first post fully, by eye, with a fillet gauge and a square, before the rest are made. I keep a record of each post: welder, date and inspection. At the end, I make sure spatter is removed, the posts are ready for coating and the records are complete.
markingPoints: Reads the drawing; checks the WPS and WPQs
Orders and checks materials
Uses a jig and easy positions
Controls distortion of the base plates
Inspects the first post and records every post

essays.stem: Explain what causes arc blow when GMAW welding pipe and plate on DC, and the ways a welder can control it.
essays.modelAnswer: Arc blow happens when magnetic fields around the work push the arc to one side, so it wanders, splatters and fails to fuse where it should. On DC the current always flows one way, so the field round the arc and the work is strong. It is worst near the ends of a joint, in corners and on pipe or plate that has become magnetised, for example from lifting magnets or magnetic inspection. To control it, the welder can move the work clamp to a different place, or use two clamps, so the current flows a different way. He can weld towards a heavy tack or away from the clamp, and add run-on and run-off plates at the ends. Large tacks help too. Pipe that is magnetised can be demagnetised with a coil, or have the cable wrapped round it to cancel the field. A shorter arc helps the welder keep control.
markingPoints: Explains arc blow as magnetic deflection of the arc
Says why DC and magnetised work make it worse
Moving or adding work clamps
Welding direction, tacks and end plates
Demagnetising pipe or wrapping the cable; short arc

practical1.title: GMAW single-V groove test coupons in 10 mm carbon steel plate in the 3G and 4G positions on ceramic backing, with bend tests and WPQ records
practical1.brief: Your group is given a GMAW WPS for a single-V groove weld in 10 mm carbon steel plate on ceramic backing, with the transfer mode it names (short-circuit or pulsed). The assessor tells each member to weld either a 3G (vertical up) or a 4G (overhead) coupon, so both positions are covered. Each member bevels or checks the plates, cleans them, sets the gap, fixes the ceramic backing, tacks, and fixes the coupon in the stand. Before welding, one member checks each set with a meter at the arc and records the wire speed, voltage and gas flow on the group's record sheet. Each member then welds the root, fill and cap to the WPS without moving the coupon, cleaning between passes. After welding, members remove the backing, inspect another member's coupon by eye and record the result. The assessor chooses two coupons for face and root bends (or side bends), and the group marks out and grinds the strips. Each member fills in a draft WPQ. Photograph each stage below.
materials: 10 mm carbon steel plate, bevelled, two pieces per member (as the assessor sets)
Ceramic backing tape for the joint length
GMAW sets with solid wire (about 1.0 mm) and argon/CO2 gas, as the WPS lists
A checked clamp meter or voltmeter, and a flowmeter for the nozzle
Welding stands that hold coupons in 3G and 4G
Grinder, wire brush, bevel gauge, weld gauge and anti-spatter
WPS, record sheet and blank WPQ forms (from the assessor)
Saw and guided bend jig (used by the assessor or under direct supervision)
photos: A tacked coupon with the ceramic backing fixed
The meter reading taken at the arc and the record sheet
Each coupon fixed in its stand in 3G or 4G
A root after the backing is removed
Finished caps on every member's coupon, with numbers showing
checklist: Prepared, gapped and backed the joint to the WPS
Set the machine to the WPS and recorded real values
Kept the coupon in the stated position for the whole test
Welded a fused root and fill with the arc kept on the front of the pool
Laid a cap with no undercut, overlap or heavy spatter
Inspected another member's coupon and recorded it correctly
Completed a draft WPQ for his or her own test
safety: Wear full PPE, with a cap and closed collar for overhead welding
Never point the gun at anyone while inching the wire
Weld only in screened bays with extraction on; chain cylinders upright
Follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules

practical2.title: GMAW open-root pipe butt coupon in the 5G position and a pipe-to-plate fillet in 5F, with visual inspection, macro etches and a PQR-style record
practical2.brief: Your group is given a GMAW WPS for an open-root carbon steel pipe butt joint (short-circuit root, as the WPS gives) and a WPS for a pipe-to-plate fillet. The group plans who does what: each member welds part of the work. Two or three members each weld one 5G pipe butt coupon (pipe fixed horizontal), with the direction the WPS gives; the others each weld one pipe-to-plate fillet in 5F (pipe fixed horizontal on the plate). Members not welding at a given time act as recorder, writing the real wire speed, voltage, gas flow and arc times on the group's PQR-style sheet. All work is inspected by eye inside and out (with a mirror for the pipe root). The group then cuts one pipe coupon and one pipe-to-plate fillet at the places the assessor marks, and grinds and etches the cut faces under supervision. The group writes a short report saying whether the welds meet the WPS and what should change. Photograph each stage below.
materials: Bevelled carbon steel pipe pieces, about 75–115 mm outside diameter
Short pipe pieces and steel plates for the pipe-to-plate fillets
GMAW sets with about 0.9–1.0 mm solid wire and argon/CO2 gas
Pipe stands for 5G and 5F, and a square
Hi-lo gauge, gap gauge, fillet gauge, mirror and grinder
Saw, abrasive papers and etching solution with its SDS (used under supervision)
WPS sheets and a blank PQR-style record and report sheet (from the assessor)
photos: A pipe coupon fitted and tacked, with the gap gauge showing
A pipe-to-plate joint set square and tacked
Finished pipe root seen from inside with the mirror
Etched cut faces from the pipe and the pipe-to-plate weld
The completed record sheet and report
checklist: Fitted and tacked the joint to the WPS and checked it with gauges
Welded in the WPS direction with a steady stick-out and even penetration
Changed the gun angle round the pipe and kept even legs on the fillet
Recorded real settings correctly when acting as recorder
Took part in cutting and etching safely and read the macros correctly
Helped write a report with a clear decision on the WPS
safety: Clamp pipe stands firmly; chock loose pipe so it cannot roll
